parts.words: It helps a small hotel get its returning guests to book direct, instead of paying a booking site to meet them again.
By the end you'll be able to take four numbers from a small property and know what it can honestly pay for the job, and whether that's worth your time.
Which brings us to the question. The site introduces the guest and keeps the guest's email.
When that guest comes back, who at the inn is paid to make sure the second booking comes to the inn? And if the answer is nobody, can somebody from outside get paid to do it?
I think it can be sold from outside. But only for what it recovers, and what it recovers is a number. By the end you'll be able to compute it for any inn.
Fair question here. If the parts to fix this are cheap, why doesn't the inn just do it?
I could not find anyone selling it to the twenty room inn. It's that the inn can only pay what the job recovers, and nobody selling this has published what that is.
That's where the old version of this argument stops.
It's the wrong number, because the inn is never going to move all of it. It needs the sites. The real question is what a recovery service can shift.
I spent ten years in hospitality, including Ace Hotel and Standard Hotels. I know this business from the inside out.
I haven't sold this particular service, though. What a thirty room inn will pay for it is still something I'd have to test.
Those are hypotheses, not a funnel, and I won't invent a conversion rate to make them look like one.
That's a side income. It's a foothold. It is not a living. Up the band it becomes a business.
My verdict is build. Bounded. The problem is real, documented from four directions. The buyer is direct. The parts are cheap.
And the arithmetic at the bottom of the band is thin, and I've told you so. So build the audit, because the audit is the test, and it costs you three properties and a month.
What I'm not saying is that a twenty room inn will pay you. Nobody knows that yet, including me. You'll know by day thirty.
The first move costs you an afternoon. Find one innkeeper you already know. Ask for four numbers. Run the ceiling.
Tell them what you found, and ask if they'd pay you to fix it. Not to close them. To find out, in one conversation, whether this business exists at their size.
Right now nobody knows. If you want more businesses worked all the way down to the number that decides them, leave a like, and subscribe for the next one.
